solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Poison barrister, oddly withdrawn and not entirely pleasant

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters of barrister are taken away, leaving the even ones
the word for pleasant is not given in full, losing its last letter

parts.note: pleasant means nice

explanation.surface: A barrister behaving strangely and coldly is accused of being a poisoner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly withdrawn' removes the 1st, 3rd, 5th... letters of BARRISTER, leaving ARSE; 'not entirely' trims NICE to NIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Arsenic is a classic toxic element, the poisoner's favourite in many mysteries.

clue.text: Seaweed from coastal Galway

indicators.note: from means the letters are taken out of the words that follow

explanation.surface: Seaweed gathered on the shore of Galway.
explanation.definitionFit: Seaweeds are large marine forms of these simple water plants.

clue.text: Strike half failing, trade union's under a cloud

indicators.note: in a down answer, under means the next piece is written below
half of the word strike fails, leaving only its first three letters

parts.note: TU is short for trade union, and the 's adds S

explanation.surface: A strike partly collapses and the union is left under suspicion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'under a cloud' reads as a phrase meaning in disgrace; 'cloud' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a low grey sheet-like type of cloud formation.

clue.text: Idiot's new, back-to-back articles

parts.note: the article an set back to back with itself, the second copy reversed, gives these letters

explanation.surface: A fool has new writing on matching pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: AN and its mirror NA placed back to back make ANNA. The answer is a variant spelling of NANA, British slang for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: Nana is informal British slang for a silly person or fool.

clue.text: Periodically acerbic and quite outrageous review

indicators.note: periodically means taking letters at regular intervals, here every second one
outrageous suggests wild disorder, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A scathing, shocking newspaper review.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Periodically' gives CRI, the 2nd, 4th and 6th letters of ACERBIC; 'outrageous' rearranges QUITE as TIQUE.
explanation.definitionFit: A critical assessment of a book or work of art is a review.

clue.text: Company with inventor of phone that locates roaming animal

parts.note: Alexander Graham Bell is credited with inventing the telephone

explanation.surface: A firm teams up with the telephone's inventor to track down wandering livestock.
explanation.definitionFit: A bell hung round a grazing beast's neck lets its owner find it by the sound when it strays.

clue.text: Box containing English produce

indicators.note: containing means the box holds the next letter

parts.note: a crate is a box

explanation.surface: A box of English fruit and vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: 'produce' suggests farm goods in the box; it is the verb meaning make.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring something into being is to make or generate it.

clue.text: Used to be a Munster laundry worker

parts.note: was is the past of be
Herman Munster is the head of the family in the American TV comedy The Munsters

explanation.surface: Someone from the Irish province of Munster once worked in a laundry.
explanation.walkthrough: Munster looks like the Irish province; it is the family in the 1960s American sitcom The Munsters, headed by Herman.
explanation.definitionFit: A man employed to do washing, especially in former times, worked in the laundry.

clue.text: Rebelliously sport zero hair, making entrance

indicators.note: to rebel is to revolt or turn over, so the pieces are written backwards

parts.note: RU is rugby union, a sport
O looks like zero
a mane is a head of hair

explanation.surface: Rebels flaunting shaven heads make their grand arrival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entrance' is the verb (en-TRANCE), meaning captivate, not a way in.
explanation.definitionFit: To entrance someone is to charm or captivate them, filling them with love.

clue.text: Addition to staff took charge of German course

parts.note: led means took charge of
a line is a course or route

explanation.surface: A new employee ran a German language course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'staff' is the musical stave; this short line extends it for notes above or below.
explanation.definitionFit: In music notation a short extra line is added above or below the five-line stave for high or low notes.

clue.text: The Queen and German don give part of speech in Latin

indicators.note: to don is to put on, so the word give wears the other pieces inside it

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen
und is German for and

explanation.surface: The monarch and a German academic hand over a grammatical term from Latin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'don' looks like a university teacher, but it is the verb: GIVE puts on ER and UND, making G-ERUND-IVE.
explanation.definitionFit: In Latin grammar this verbal adjective expresses necessity, as in 'Carthago delenda est'.

clue.text: Schoolkid on vacation trapping brown bear

indicators.note: trapping means the outer letters enclose the next piece
vacated, the word schoolkid is emptied of everything but its first and last letters

parts.note: tan is a brown colour

explanation.surface: A child on school holiday catches a brown bear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bear' looks like the animal tied to 'brown', but it is the verb meaning put up with.
explanation.definitionFit: To bear something is to tolerate or put up with it, as in 'I can't stand him'.

clue.text: Changing lane, hooted and hit battered bangers

indicators.note: changing the order of these letters rearranges them into a new phrase

explanation.surface: A motorist switches lanes, sounds the horn and crashes into some battered old cars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bangers' are British slang for both old cars and sausages; this dish is sausages baked in Yorkshire pudding batter.
explanation.definitionFit: The British dish is sausages cooked in batter, bangers being everyday slang for sausages.

clue.text: Large amount of champagne and drug-taking upset Shakespeare's prince

parts.note: meth is short for methamphetamine, a drug
use, the taking of a drug

indicators.note: upset means overturned, so in a down answer these letters are read upwards

parts.note: Prince Hal is the future Henry V in Shakespeare's Henry IV plays

explanation.surface: Bubbly and drug use have upset a Shakespearean royal.
explanation.definitionFit: A bottle size of champagne holding eight standard bottles is named after the biblical patriarch.

clue.text: Provide cover for unhorsed jockeys

indicators.note: to jockey is to manoeuvre or shift around, so these letters are moved into a new order

explanation.surface: Riders who have fallen off need protecting.
explanation.definitionFit: To wrap something entirely, as in a shroud, is to provide it with a covering.

clue.text: Move around on Scottish island and get lost, finally

parts.note: re means on or about
Arran is an island in the Firth of Clyde

indicators.note: the word get loses its final letter

explanation.surface: Travelling about a Scottish island, someone ends up getting lost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get lost, finally' takes the last letter off GET.
explanation.definitionFit: To shift items into a new order or position is to reorder or reorganise them.

clue.text: Unconcerned about right and wrong marks in a viva

indicators.note: in means the first piece goes inside the next

parts.note: a viva is an oral examination
M is short for mark or marks, the old German currency

explanation.surface: An examiner's marks in an oral exam show indifference to ethics.
explanation.walkthrough: M (marks, the old German currency) sits inside A + ORAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone without any moral sense does not care whether conduct is good or bad.

clue.text: Fifty of us in school are doing really well

indicators.note: in means these letters go inside the next word

parts.note: a school is a group of fish, so school suggests fish
L is the Roman numeral fifty
our means of us, belonging to us

explanation.surface: Fifty of our pupils are thriving at school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'school' suggests pupils, but it stands for FISH, which swim in schools.
explanation.definitionFit: To thrive or prosper is to do very well; the verb fits the plural subject.

clue.text: Book of Numbers referred to in church?

definitions.text: Book of Numbers referred to in church?

parts.words: Book of Numbers referred to in church?
parts.note: not the Old Testament book: in church the vicar announces each song by its number in this book

explanation.surface: Seems to be the fourth book of the Bible being cited in a service.
explanation.walkthrough: Numbers looks like the Old Testament book; here it means the numbered songs a congregation is told to turn to.
explanation.definitionFit: A hymn book holds numbered songs, which are announced by number during services.

clue.text: Liable to get lost, maybe, in trees with son

parts.note: maples are trees

explanation.surface: A boy might wander off and lose himself in the woods.
explanation.definitionFit: Without a chart to navigate by, a traveller may well go astray.

clue.text: Staple factory, Scot's own

parts.note: a plant is an industrial works or factory
ain is the Scots word for own

explanation.surface: A works making staples belongs to a Scotsman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staple' suggests the office fastener made in a factory; it is a basic food.
explanation.definitionFit: This starchy banana-like fruit is a basic food in much of the tropics.

clue.text: Gold thread primarily used in fashion house, one hears

parts.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold

indicators.note: used in means the letter is put inside the next piece

parts.note: Dior is a famous Paris fashion house

indicators.note: primarily means only the first letter of thread is taken

explanation.surface: Gold thread is used by a designer label, so people say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one hears' looks like a sound signal; it is the definition, a listener (Latin audire).
explanation.definitionFit: An auditor in the old sense is a listener, from the Latin for hear.

clue.text: Criticises batting performances

definitions.meaning: to knock something is to run it down
in cricket an innings is informally a knock

explanation.surface: A cricket commentator finds fault with the innings played.
explanation.definitionFit: Knocks means disparages, and in cricket a batsman's innings is called a knock.

clue.text: Old Sauterne, pud, and endless fizz

indicators.note: to fizz is to bubble and froth, so the letters are churned into a new order
endless means the word and loses its final letter

explanation.surface: An aged dessert wine, pudding and some sparkling drink make a dinner menu.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' cuts AND to AN; SAUTERNE + PUD + AN are rearranged ('fizz').
explanation.definitionFit: Someone pensioned off or past their usefulness is too aged to carry on.

clue.text: Nominal fine ten pounds

indicators.note: pounds as in batters its way in, so the first piece is driven into the second

parts.note: taken as written
OK means fine

explanation.surface: A ten-pound penalty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pounds' looks like money; it drives OK into TEN.
explanation.definitionFit: A token payment is a merely nominal, symbolic amount.

clue.text: Vintage Times puzzle

parts.note: a cru is a vineyard or vintage of wine
X is the multiplication sign, times

explanation.surface: An old crossword from this very newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times puzzle' suggests the newspaper's crossword; Times is the sign X.
explanation.definitionFit: The central difficulty or knotty problem in a matter is its puzzle.

clue.text: One regularly stopping Hutton perhaps staying in bed

indicators.note: regularly means the interruption is repeated at regular intervals, after each of the name's first two letters
stopping means the letter for one plugs a gap inside the cricketer's name

parts.note: Len Hutton was a famous England cricket captain
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone keeps interrupting a cricketer, who stays under the covers.
explanation.walkthrough: I goes into LEN twice, at regular intervals: L-I-E-I-N. Sir Len Hutton was an English Test batsman.
explanation.definitionFit: A lie-in is a lazy morning spent in bed past the usual hour of rising.

clue.text: Credit starts to be refused to Dick, Peter and Grace?

indicators.note: the opening letter of each of the two names is denied them, so both lose their beginnings

explanation.surface: A lender refuses credit to two men and a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grace' seems a woman's name beside Dick and Peter; it is W. G. Grace, the great Victorian English cricketer, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: W. G. Grace is the most famous example of a Victorian player of the bat-and-ball game.

clue.text: Society girl pursuing house party organiser

indicators.note: pursuing means following, so these pieces come after the first

parts.note: Tess is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A debutante chases after a house, where a party's being thrown.
explanation.definitionFit: The woman who throws a gathering and entertains guests arranges the festivities.

clue.text: Hard object audibly strains legendary guitarist

parts.note: H is short for hard, as on pencils
an end is an aim or object

indicators.note: audibly means what follows is said out loud, giving a different spelling

parts.note: ricks are strains or sprains

explanation.surface: A tough item, heard straining, recalls a famous rock musician.
explanation.walkthrough: RICKS (strains, as in a ricked back) is said aloud to give RIX.
explanation.definitionFit: Jimi Hendrix is widely hailed as the greatest rock electric player of all time.
